Shanghai Overseas Chinese Federation - meeting cancelled
by order of the French Police

Following the receipt of an order from the French
Police at 10 p.m. May 18, the Shanghai Overseas Chinese
Federation, with an office at No. 80 Paris Terrace,
off Avenue Dubail, cancelled the meeting which was to
have been held at 2 p.m. May 18 in the Chinese Y.M.C.A.
building, 123 Boulevard de Montigny.

The Federation will convene a meeting at 1 p.m. May
25, in the Chinese Chamber of Commerce, North Soochow
Road, when representatives of various public bodies will
be invited to attend.

Shanghai Overseas Chinese Federation - publishes booklet

The Shanghai Overseas Chinese Federation, No. 80
Paris Terrace, Avenue Dubail, has published a booklet
entitled "A Tragic Review of the Oppression of Overseas
Chinese by the Government of Siam." This booklet contains
the following articles:-

1. The Emigration Law promulgated to limit the number
of Chinese entering Siam.

2. Measures for the enforcement of compulsory naturali-
zation.

3. The business of Overseas Chinese is ruined.

4. Control is exercised over the thoughts and speeches
of the Chinese.

5. Innocent Overseas Chinese are slaughtered.

6. Formal relations should be established between China
and Siam.

Subject (in full) Arrest of three ex-seamen in Wayside District on Oct. 2/3,
1934 on Warrants applied for by the Public Safety Bureau.
Made by D. S. Sansom Forwarded by [Signature] D./.

The three Cantonese ex-seamen , Zia Zuh Sung ( 謝
日生 ) alias Lau Wu ( 老吳 ), Dung Yau ( 鄧堯 )
alias Lau Tseu ( 老周 ) and Zung Liang ( 陳良
蔣成文)
alias Chiang Zung Vung, arrested on October 2/3, 1934 at
different addresses in Wayside District, have been closely
questioned regarding their association with the Communist Party
as alleged by the Public Safety Bureau.

Communist literature was seized at the homes of
the 2nd. and 3rd. accused, whilst the 1st. accused has been
identified as an acquaintance of the 3rd. accused.

The 2nd. accused, Dung Yau alias Lau Tseu, admits
that during the last five months or so he has been the custodian
of literature deposited at his home by his supervisors Lin Han
( 林漢 ) and Tsai ( 蔡 ). The literature deals with
communism in general and refers to anti-Japanese movements and
activities among seamen. In addition to this work, the
2nd. accused visited all the steamers of the Blue Funnel Line
arriving in this port and maintained a liaison between
Cantonese members of the crews and communist agents ashore.

Documentary evidence tends to indicate that
subversive literature is being regularly distributed aboard
steamers of the "Dollar", "C.P.R.", "Blue Funnel" and "Java-
China-Japan" Lines through members of the crews who appear
to be in constant touch with certain communist agents locally.
The names of the individuals concerned are not revealed in the
seized documents.

No evidence can be obtained to show any connection
between the Chun Loh Club, 303 Woochang Road, and this phase
of communistic activity.

Zia Zuh Sung (徐祖生)
Canton                                      D.S. Sansom
Special Br.          3/10/34                Clerk Chao Shih-chow.

My name is Zia Zuh Sung, age 32, Cantonese, single,
unemployed ship's fireman, last residing at 955 Seward Road.
    I first came to Shanghai about 2 months ago, coming
from Hongkong. I arrived here on a Blue Funnel Steamer,
having been employed aboard as a fireman. I have been em-
ployed on steamers for the past 10 years. Whenever I became
temporarily unemployed I resided at the Seamen's Club, Hongkong.
    On my arrival at Shanghai, I left the steamer (name
unknown) voluntarily. I had been employed there for 4 months,
and had about $63 in my possession when I came here. My
reasons for leaving the ship were that I preferred to sell
provisions to members of ships' crews on a commission. I had
no friends in Shanghai on my arrival. I first stayed in a
hotel (name forgotten) in the French Concession. I then took
up residence at 955 Seward Road. Since then I have been
regularly occupied at selling provisions aboard steamers of
the Blue Funnel Line in particular. My acquaintance with men
aboard these boats led to me accompanying some of them to my
house for recreation purposes only. I have no acquaintances
in Shanghai. I have not been to Lane 131, 77 Tongahan Road.
I do not know any occupant of this address and I have no
knowledge of any communistic literature having been found
there. A tenant at that address who identified me as a fre-
quenter of the place has made a mistake.
    I have never been a member of the Seamen's Union
and I am not interested in any political movement whatsoever.
    This statement is true.
                                        (Sd.) Zia Zuh Sung.

Dung Yao (鄧堯)
Canton                                      D.S. Sansom
Special Br.          3/10/34                Clerk Chao Shih-chow.

My name is Dung Yao, age 28, Cantonese, single,
unemployed, last residing at 106 San Kwan Dong Loong,eward
Road.

I came to Shanghai in April 1934 from Hongkong where
I had resided for about 4 years, during which period I made
occasional visits to my home in Canton. At Hongkong I worked
as a hawker, and the visits to Canton were for the purpose
of working on a farm when business became bad in Hongkong.
Eventually I obtained employment as a fireman on the "Kut-
sang" (吉生), which brought me to Shanghai. On arrival here
I went to the Lin Nan (嶺南) Hotel on East Woochang Road in
accordance with an arrangement of a friend named Ung Tsai
(硬仔), a Cantonese, believed to be employed in Sincere Co.,
Nanking Road, who had written to me at Hongkong. Two days
later a male Cantonese named Lin Han (林漢) called on me at
the hotel. I had not met him previously. We discussed
unemployment and Lin Han offered to accommodate me. We then
boarded a tram and after about 10 minutes we alighted, walked
for about 10 minutes and arrived at a small goods shop. I
was shown to a room which was occupied by two Chinese females,
both of whom could speak Cantonese. I do not know their names.
They allowed me to live in the same room for 10 days. Lin Han
came to the room a few times, and after 10 days he gave me
$20 and accompanied me to a house on Woochang Road where he
rented a room for me. On the instructions of Lin Han I then
associated myself with the crews of the City Government Ferry
boats which operate between the Bund and Woosung. Right up

- 2 -
to the present I have been visiting these boats practically
daily and have been hawking vegetables and fruit, etc., to
members of the crews. Actually, I took orders from them,
obtained the provisions from shops on Foochung Road and was
paid a commission. Lin Han continued to visit me at my
home on Foochang Road until the end of June when I removed
to 106 San Kwan Dong Loong, Seward Road, the place where I
was arrested, with the approval of Lin Han. Soon after this
change of residence Lin Han brought some literature and told
me retain it. He continued to visit me regularly and brought
with him another Cantonese named Tsai (蔡), previously un-
known to me. These two persons drafted documents and read
literature in my room. I was always present with them. I
read some of these drafts and discussed with them the merits
of communism. They asked me to bring friends to the room to
meet them; consequently I took about 10 Cantonese, who are
employed on Blue Funnel Line Steamers, to them. I intro-
duced these men to Tsai in particular, and he discussed with
them the oppression of the workers and the necessity for unity.
I kept contact with them, and whenever their steamers arrived
here I took them to Tsai at the Chang Kee (章记) Restaurant,
385 Foochang Road; Koon Tsin Tung Kee (冠珍通心酒樓) Restaurant,
40 Foochang Road; a teashop at 37 Hambury Road, or the Bund
Gardens. I have never heard about the Chun Loh Club. Tsai
sometimes took these men to another place, but I do not know
where. I have seen him hand to them written matter pertaining
to the Seamen's Union.

- 3 -

My school education was restricted to a period of
one year from the age of 10 when I studied at a private school
in Canton. I am able to read and write to a very limited
extent. When literature has been handed to me by Tsai or
Lin Han, they mentioned that same was of a revolutionary
character.

Since coming into contact with Lin Han, I have re-
ceived in all a sum of about $55 from him in consideration
of the work done on his behalf. In addition to this I have
received $20 from Tsai.

The only steamers I visited in the course of my
activities were of the Blue Funnel Line, moored at Pootung.
Practically all the steamers of this line were visited by me.
I am unable to give the names of the steamers. Of the indi-
viduals whom I met aboard these boats I can only remember
the names of four, to wit:- Liu Tuh (刘德), Liu Nyi (刘二),
Ho Tien (何甜) and Loh (陸). These men are employed on
different ships and I have reason to believe that they were
all firemen.

This statement is true.

(Sd.) Dung Yao.

Zung Liang (陈良)
Canton                                      D.S. Muir
Special Br.           3/10/34               Clerk Liao.

My name is Zung Liang, married, male, age 30,
native of Pau An Village (宝安), Canton. My wife is
at present residing somewhere in Canton.
    I came to Shanghai direct from Canton during the
end of 1931, and went to reside with a relative named
Tung Kung (邓根) at 25 Tuh Shing Lee of Wuchang Road.
    At the age of 14 years, I went to study under a private
tutor named Mah Ho Kiu (麦火娇) at my native village for
1 year only, previous to this I had never studied before,
so my ability to read and write is very limited.
    After completing my year's study, I went to assist
on my mother's farm as a labourer until I was 21 years of
age. At this time my uncle offered me similar employment
with an annual wage of $6 and free board and lodgings.
This I accepted. I remained in my uncle's employ for
6 years but owing to a trival financial pecuniary dispute I left
his service at the end of December, 1931, and shortly
afterwards came to Shanghai on my own accord with a view
to seeking employment.
    On arrival in Shanghai I first went to live with my
relative in Wuchang Road. I stayed here for about 8 months
during that time I was unable to obtain employment.
    On being recommended by my relative I ultimately found
employment with the Sung Kee Carpenter Shop (生记), No.201
Av. Rd. VII, but being unaccustomed to this trade was dis-
missed after 3 months. During the time of employment I was
paid $6 per month.

-2-

For the following 4 months I was again unemployed
but during this period I met one named Tong Tien Kwang
(湯天光), a wharf coolie employed at Holts Wharf, Pootung,
who introduced me to a wharf coolie contractor with a
view to obtaining employment as a coolie. I was engaged as
a wharf coolie for about 6 months at various wharves in
Hongkew District, the wharf names I don't know. I had to
give up this work as it was too strenuous for me.

Since September, 1933, I have been unemployed, and have
no regular fixed abode, at night time I slept in alleyways
and shop entrances, during the day time I wandered about the
streets and existed on the few coppers given me daily
by a Cantonese gentleman named Ching Mcu Zung (金滿堂),
who resides in Hongkew District.

In July this year, I was approached by a person named
Kuo Liang (郭亮) who appeared to be a native of a Northern
province. This man would not tell me where he resided when
I asked him.

Kuo Liang asked me if I had any employment and on
my answering in the negative, he said he would give me
food and lodgings unconditionally. I accepted his offer
and he took me to a room at No.90 Yung Khin Lee (永吉里), Ward Road.
I stayed there for about one month during this time Kuo
Liang visited me once and gave me $4 to buy food.

During August I was ordered by this same person to
remove to 77 Yuen Khin Lee (元吉里), Tongshan Road, the place where

--3--
I was arrested. I complied with his order and at this
new address Kuo Liang visited me on 3 times; the most
recent being about one week before I was arrested.
Each occasion this man visited me he brought a quantity
of communist literature, the first time he brought it
enclosed in a suit case, but on the latter two visits,
the literature was wrapped in Chinese newspaper.
The first time Kuo Liang brought communist literature
he informed me that I was to look after same and study the
contents of the literature, but up to the time of my
arrest I had only read a few that I was able.
When visiting me Kuo Liang was always unaccompanied
and came to my room about 7a.m. staying there for only
a few minutes.

(Signed) Zung Liang.
